2027-03-07.title: Fifth Sunday of the Great Fast
2027-03-07.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Hagar and the God who sees
Hewers of wood and drawers of water
Rivers of living water and the light of the world
2027-03-07.alt: Season of the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba). The fast has passed its midpoint; the fifth week begins.
2027-03-07.verse: “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink. As the scripture has said, ‘Out of the believer's heart shall flow rivers of living water.’”
theo: The first reading begins in a household that has gone wrong. Sarai, unable to bear children, had given her Egyptian slave-girl Hagar to Abram; Hagar conceived and looked down on her mistress; Sarai complained; and Abram washed his hands of it: “Your slave-girl is in your power; do to her as you please.” “Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she ran away from her.” A pregnant foreign servant, alone, runs into the desert toward Egypt. And there, of all places, “The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness.” He asks her the question the Great Fast asks each of us: “Hagar, slave-girl of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?” He promises her a son and gives him a name, Ishmael, God hears, “for the LORD has given heed to your affliction.” Then Hagar does something no one in Scripture has done before her: she gives God a name. “So she named the LORD who spoke to her, ‘You are El-roi’; for she said, ‘Have I really seen God and remained alive after seeing him?’” El-roi, the God who sees. The first person in the Bible to name God is not a patriarch or a priest, but a runaway slave woman. Thousands of women from Kerala work as housemaids and carers far from home, some of them treated harshly behind closed doors where no one sees. God sees. And he asks us whether we see them too, in our own homes, in the women who work for us, and in the women of our families whose hurts are hidden.

The second reading finishes last Friday's story. Three days after the treaty, Israel discovers that the Gibeonites are neighbours, not travellers from afar. The congregation murmurs, but the leaders hold firm: “We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we must not touch them.” An oath made in God's name is kept, even when it was obtained by a trick and even when it costs. The psalm praises the one “who stand by their oath even to their hurt” (Psalm 15:4). Our marriage vows, our baptismal promises and our word given in business are to be kept the same way. And notice how the story ends. The Gibeonites are spared, and Joshua makes them “hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD.” The outsiders who came with mouldy bread end their story beside the altar of the God of Israel. Christian readers have seen in this wood and water carried to the altar a hint of the wood of the Cross and the water of Baptism, by which God brings strangers near to his altar.

Paul now turns from the mercy of God to the life it makes possible: “I appeal to you therefore, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your minds.” This is what the Great Fast is for. We do not fast because the body is bad, but because the body is to be offered: eyes, tongue, hands, appetite and time placed on the altar with Christ. And the sacrifice is not private. “For as in one body we have many members, and not all the members have the same function, so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually we are members one of another.” Paul ends with a list that could hang on the wall of every Christian home: “Let love be genuine; hate what is evil, hold fast to what is good; love one another with mutual affection; outdo one another in showing honor. Do not lag in zeal, be ardent in spirit, serve the Lord.”

The Gospel takes us to the festival of Booths in Jerusalem. During the feast, as Jewish tradition describes it, water was carried in procession from the pool of Siloam and poured out at the altar, and great lamps were lit in the temple courts so that the whole city glowed. Into that water and that light Jesus speaks. “On the last day of the festival, the great day, while Jesus was standing there, he cried out, ‘Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink.’” John explains: “Now he said this about the Spirit, which believers in him were to receive.” Then, in the treasury near the great lamps, he says: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness but will have the light of life.” Water and light: these are the two signs of our Baptism, the Mamodisa, when we were washed in water and a burning candle was placed in our hands. At the Easter Vigil the Church will bless the water and carry the new light into a dark church, and those preparing for Baptism will receive both. Hagar found a spring in the desert and met the God who sees; the Gibeonites carried water to the altar; Christ himself is the spring from which rivers of living water flow, and the light that the darkness cannot overcome. His hour “had not yet come”, but it is coming: on the Cross water will flow from his side, and on Easter morning the light will rise.
conn: Hagar meets the angel by a spring (Genesis 16:7); later, when her child is dying of thirst, “God opened her eyes and she saw a well of water” (Genesis 21:19). At another well Jesus promises a Samaritan woman “a spring of water gushing up to eternal life” (John 4:14).
Hagar calls God El-roi, the God who sees (Genesis 16:13). Jesus teaches that the Father “who sees in secret will reward you” (Matthew 6:6).

Israel keeps the oath sworn to Gibeon (Joshua 9:19); the psalm blesses those “who stand by their oath even to their hurt” (Psalm 15:4). Centuries later God avenged the Gibeonites when Saul broke that oath (2 Samuel 21:1–2).
The Gibeonites become hewers of wood and drawers of water for the altar (Joshua 9:27). The Son of Man “came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45).
Ezekiel sees water flowing from below the threshold of the temple, south of the altar (Ezekiel 47:1). Jesus is the new temple; from his pierced side “blood and water came out” (John 19:34).
“The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2). In Christ “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it” (John 1:5).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana our bodies, our work and our fasting are placed with Christ on the altar as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God.
The Holy Qurbana is the spring of living water in the desert of the fast: the Spirit is poured out, and the Lord who is the light of the world gives himself as food.
outline: Ask: where have I come from, and where am I going?
The God who sees a runaway slave woman in the desert.
Point 2 · Wood and water for the altar
An oath kept, and outsiders brought near.
Bodies offered, minds renewed, love genuine.
The feast of Booths, and the signs of our Baptism.
A spring in the desert, and a candle carried into a dark church at Easter.
“Let anyone who is thirsty come to me.”
live: Notice one person this week who works for you or serves you unseen: a domestic worker, a driver, a cleaner. Thank them by name, pay them justly, and pray for them.
Fulfil one promise you have delayed, to God, to your spouse, to a child or to a colleague.
Choose one discipline for eyes, tongue or hands this week and offer it each morning as a living sacrifice.
Find out the date of your Baptism, light a candle at home that evening, and renew your baptismal promises as a family.
fathers: How can the body become a sacrifice? Let the eye look on nothing evil, and it has become a sacrifice; let the tongue speak nothing shameful, and it has become an offering; let the hand do nothing unlawful, and it has become a whole burnt offering. And let the hand also do good, giving alms, so that the sacrifice is complete.

The Lord cries out: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. We come to him not by walking but by believing, not with the feet but with love. Whoever drinks from him becomes himself a spring, for love overflows from the heart to others.
magis: The moral life is spiritual worship: we present our bodies as a living sacrifice, and in the Eucharist this offering is nourished.
Water is a sign of the Holy Spirit; the Spirit is the living water welling up from Christ crucified, in whom we drink.
Contemplation is a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus: “I look at him and he looks at me.”
An oath takes God as witness to what one affirms; it calls on divine truthfulness as a pledge of one's own.
Baptism is called enlightenment, because the baptised become children of light, and indeed light themselves.
saints: 8–13 Mar: fifth week of the Great Fast. 12 Mar: Fifth Friday of the Great Fast (abstinence; Way of the Cross). In the Latin calendar St John of God (8 Mar) and St Frances of Rome (9 Mar) are commemorated.
2027-03-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, spring of living water and light of the world, you are El-roi, the God who saw Hagar in the desert and who sees us now. See the hidden sufferings of the poor, the servants and the strangers, and teach us to see them with your eyes. Make us faithful to our word, bring near to your altar all who are far away, and receive our bodies as a living sacrifice. Pour out your Spirit like rivers in our hearts, and let us walk in your light until we come to the light of Easter. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

quick: Hagar, a runaway slave, meets God by a spring and names him El-roi, the God who sees.
Israel keeps its oath to Gibeon, and the outsiders end up serving at the altar.
Present your bodies as a living sacrifice; Jesus is the living water and the light of the world.
2027-03-07.action: Thank by name one person who serves you unseen, and pay them justly.
2027-03-07.question: Where have I come from, where am I going, and whom have I failed to see?
catechism: The living sacrifice of the moral life.
Water, sign of the Holy Spirit.
I look at him and he looks at me.
kidsaint: They died for Jesus in Carthage, in North Africa, on 7 March 203. Perpetua was a young mother from a noble family; Felicity was a slave who gave birth to a baby girl in prison just before they died. In the world one was a lady and the other a servant, but in Jesus they were sisters, and they gave each other the kiss of peace before they died. Lesson: in God's family no one is less important than anyone else!
2027-03-07.special: Fifth Sunday of the Great Fast.
term: A Hebrew name for God given by Hagar in Genesis 16:13, usually understood as “the God who sees” or “the God who sees me”. It reminds us that no suffering is hidden from God.

family.explain: Hagar was a servant girl. She was treated badly, so she ran away into the desert, all alone, with a baby on the way. But God found her beside a spring of water! He spoke kindly to her and promised to look after her and her baby. Hagar gave God a beautiful name: the God who sees me. God sees you too, always, wherever you are.
family.intention: We pray for women and children who are treated badly and feel that no one sees them.
family.ask: Ask: “Who works for us or helps us that we hardly ever notice? How can we thank them this week?”

illus: A woman from Kottayam worked for eleven years as a housemaid in a Gulf city. In one house she was not allowed to go out, and she ate alone in the kitchen after everyone else. Every night she prayed with a small picture of the Sacred Heart hidden in her suitcase. Years later, back in Kerala, she told her parish prayer group: “I thought nobody in the world could see me. But I knew one thing. God saw me. That is how I lived.” When she finished, a young mother in the group went home and, for the first time, sat down to eat with the woman who cleaned her house.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are the God who sees, the living water and the light of the world. See us now, and let us see you. Amen.
share: Hagar, where have you come from and where are you going? (Genesis 16:8). Where is my life heading this Lent?
We have sworn to them by the LORD; we must not touch them (Joshua 9:19). What promise have I failed to keep?
Present your bodies as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1). What part of myself have I not yet offered to God?
Let anyone who is thirsty come to me (John 7:37). What am I thirsty for, and where am I looking for it?
interc: For the Church, that she may be a spring in the desert for all who are thirsty.
For domestic workers, migrants and all who are mistreated behind closed doors.
For husbands and wives, that they may keep their vows even when it costs.
For those preparing for Baptism this Easter, that they may receive the living water and the light.
For our parish, that we may love genuinely and serve the Lord with ardent spirit.
pm.close: Father, you saw Hagar in the desert and you sent your Son as living water and light. See all who suffer unseen, make us faithful to our word, and let our lives be a living sacrifice pleasing to you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, Hagar was a servant, a foreigner and a pregnant woman, treated harshly and alone in the desert. But the angel of the Lord found her by a spring of water and asked: where have you come from and where are you going? (Genesis 16:8). That is the question of the Great Fast for each of us.

Hagar gave God a name: El-roi, the God who sees (Genesis 16:13). The first person in the Bible to name God was a runaway slave woman. God sees those whom no one sees. Let us ask him to give us his eyes for the servants, the migrants and the hidden sufferers around us.

Israel discovered that the Gibeonites had tricked them, yet the leaders said: we have sworn to them by the Lord, and we must not touch them (Joshua 9:19). They kept their word even when it cost. Our vows and promises must be kept the same way. And the outsiders ended up carrying wood and water for the altar of the Lord: God brings strangers near.

Paul says: present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God (Romans 12:1). That is why we fast. Our eyes, tongue, hands and time are placed on the altar with Christ, and we are transformed by the renewing of our minds.

At the feast of Booths, when water was poured at the altar and great lamps lit up the temple, Jesus cried out: let anyone who is thirsty come to me; and he said: I am the light of the world (John 7:37; 8:12). Water and light are the signs of our Baptism.

This week, let us see one person we have overlooked, keep one promise we have delayed, offer one discipline as a living sacrifice, and come thirsty to Jesus. At Easter he will give us the living water and the light. Amen.
kids: Children, Hagar was alone in the desert and thought nobody cared. But God found her and she called him: the God who sees me! God sees you too, when you are happy and when you are sad.
Jesus said: if you are thirsty, come to me. He is like a spring of fresh water and a bright light in the dark. When you see water or a candle this week, remember Jesus!

intro: Theme: “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink.”
Hagar and the God who sees, an oath kept and strangers brought to the altar, the living sacrifice, and Christ the living water and the light of the world.

I appeal to you therefore, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.

concl: The God who saw Hagar sees us; the God who brought the Gibeonites to his altar brings us near; the Son pours out the Spirit like rivers and shines as the light of the world.
Let us see the unseen, keep our word, offer our bodies, and come thirsty to Christ.
2027-03-07.resolve: This week, thank one unseen servant by name, keep one delayed promise, and renew your baptismal promises with a lit candle.
